prompt: What is the daily stand-up for?

choices.why: If everybody faces one outsider, it has become that.
Right. A blocked card is noticed on the day.
Problems are named there and solved after.

choices.text: Estimating the tickets in to do
choices.why: Estimating belongs in refinement.

prompt: When walking the board, where does the stand-up start?

choices.text: At to do, with what to start
choices.why: Starting is discussed last.
It goes by card, not by person.
Done needs nothing; it is not discussed.
Right. Then in progress, then to do.

prompt: Which stand-up update is most useful to the team?
hint: Does it name a card and ask for something?

choices.why: True, and it tells the team nothing.
Right. A card, and a request somebody can act on.

choices.text: I was very busy all day
choices.why: Busy is not information about the work.
It hides whatever might be stuck.

prompt: Two people start discussing how to fix the payment bug during the stand-up. What should happen?
hint: Named in the daily, solved after it.

choices.text: Let them finish; it is important
choices.why: It is important to them, in front of everyone else.

choices.text: Take it after, with only those two
choices.why: Right. The parking lot.
The topic is fine; the timing is not.

choices.text: Extend the daily to thirty minutes
choices.why: That costs everybody for two people's problem.

prompt: A daily stand-up takes about ___ minutes.
What does sprint planning produce? Choose all that apply.

choices.why: Yes. One sentence.
Yes. The tickets the team agrees it can finish.
That is an input; refinement produces it.

choices.text: A release date for each ticket
choices.why: It plans a sprint, not a date per ticket.

prompt: Normal velocity is 30 points, and only 35 of 40 working days are available this sprint. What does the team plan?

choices.why: Five days are missing.
A plan filled to the last point breaks on the first surprise.
More than it can finish means finishing less.
Right. 26 by capacity, minus room for the unexpected.

prompt: Who decides how much fits in the sprint?

choices.why: They propose the goal and order the backlog.
Right. They pull tickets until capacity.
They say what matters, not how much fits.
Nobody outside decides how much the team can do.

prompt: In planning, nobody can explain what a ticket needs. What happens to it?

choices.text: It goes in; details come later
choices.why: That is how #35 happened.
Right. What cannot be explained cannot be started.

choices.text: The most senior person takes it
choices.why: Seniority does not answer the open questions.
It may be important; it is just not ready.

prompt: Match each meeting to what it looks at.

pairs.right: The product, working, with the people who asked
How the team worked, by the team alone
What is in the way today

prompt: At the review, the owner asks for the confirmation to repeat the pickup time. What happens to that request?
hint: It was found early, which is the point.

choices.text: It becomes a ticket on the backlog
choices.why: Right. Found two weeks in, not months after release.

choices.text: Ana changes it during the meeting
choices.why: Work goes through a ticket and a review.

choices.text: It is ignored until the next release
choices.why: Feedback is why the review exists.

choices.text: The sprint is extended to include it
choices.why: The sprint ends; the next one can take it.

prompt: Why show only finished work at the review?
hint: Half done can look nearly done.

choices.why: It is visible on the board.
Length is not the reason.

choices.text: It avoids feedback on unready work
choices.why: Right. And it does not look done when it is not.
It is about what is finished, not about code.

hint: What makes people say what went wrong?

choices.why: Comfort is a side effect; honesty is the goal.
People do; the retro asks why the process let them through.

choices.text: People then admit what went wrong
choices.why: Right. And the process gets fixed, not a person.
Who attends is a separate question.

prompt: A retro lists eight problems. How many actions should the team take on?
hint: Changes that happen beat changes that do not.

choices.text: One or two, each with an owner
choices.why: Right. The rest can wait for the next retro.
Eight at once usually means none happen.
A retro without actions changes nothing.
The team picks its own actions.

prompt: What should a retrospective start with?

choices.why: Right. Did they happen, and did they help?

choices.text: A list of who was late, and why
choices.why: That is blame, and the retro avoids it.
Numbers can inform, but actions come first.
That belongs to planning.

prompt: A team wonders whether it still needs a weekly meeting. What question does the lesson suggest?
hint: The question the lesson opened with.

choices.text: Does everybody on the team enjoy it?
choices.why: Enjoyment is not the test.

choices.text: Is it in the Scrum Guide?
choices.why: The guide does not know this team.

choices.text: What would go wrong without it?
choices.why: Right. If nobody can say, try a sprint without it.
Age says nothing about value.

prompt: Put a sprint's meetings in order, from its first morning to its last afternoon.
trap: A retro before the review changes the process before seeing what the sprint delivered.
